tldr: To scale up tactile-enabled robot manipulation, the authors introduce N0-Foundation, a foundational paradigm integrating NeoData (a 30,000+ hour large-scale visuo-tactile dataset), NeoForce (a model unifying contact forces as a shared representation), and standardized benchmarks spanning real robots and simulation.
hero_caption: An overview of N0-Foundation. It integrates tactile-enabled collection hardware, the large-scale visuo-tactile NeoData dataset spanning over 30,000 hours and 450 tasks, a unified tactile representation model based on force fields, and evaluation benchmarks pairing real robots (NeoReal) with simulation (NeoSim).
overview:
Recent advances in robot learning have been driven by large-scale behavioral data and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, existing datasets rely predominantly on camera images, largely omitting tactile information such as contact states, fine force regulation, and onset of slip. As a result, delicate tasks like deformable object manipulation (fabric, paper) or high-precision assembly (inserting parts) remain difficult. Worse, tactile sensors differ widely across manufacturers and sensing principles, creating a severe fragmentation problem that makes it hard to pool data for unified training.

To solve this, the authors built N0-Foundation, an end-to-end framework spanning hardware, data collection, unified representation learning, and standardized evaluation benchmarks. First, they developed a durable vision-based tactile sensor alongside N0-TacUMI, a handheld device for agile data collection. Together with 5 real robot embodiments, they gathered NeoData, a visuo-tactile dataset exceeding 30,000 hours and 1.4 million episodes. Furthermore, to overcome device-specific visual appearances, they proposed NeoForce, a tactile representation model that learns 3-axis force fields (shear and pressure) across the contact surface as a shared physical language.

Evaluating on a benchmark suite of 10 real-world tasks (NeoReal) and 12 simulation tasks (NeoSim), tactile-aware policies demonstrated substantial gains in success rates over vision-only baselines. Crucially, feeding the policy unified 3-axis physical force fields proved distinctly more effective than providing raw tactile images directly.
contributions: Established N0-Foundation, an end-to-end tactile-centric embodied intelligence paradigm integrating hardware, large-scale data collection, representation learning, and standardized evaluation.

Engineered N0-TacUMI, a handheld collection device equipped with vision-based tactile sensors, and built NeoData (including its open-source subset OpenNeoData)—a visuo-tactile dataset spanning over 30,000 hours and 450 tasks collected via both real robots and handheld demonstrations.

Developed NeoForce, a visuo-tactile representation model that learns a dense 3-axis force field across the contact surface as a shared supervision space, abstracting away sensor-specific visual artifacts.
Constructed a comprehensive standardized benchmark dedicated to contact-rich manipulation, comprising 10 real-robot tasks (NeoReal) and 12 simulation tasks (NeoSim).

sections.heading: Can tactile sensing break through the physical contact barrier?
sections.summary: While vision-driven large-scale learning has advanced rapidly, delicate contact-rich manipulation remains hindered because contact forces and slip cannot be directly seen. Incompatible tactile sensor specifications have also prevented cross-device data reuse. N0-Foundation tackles these challenges end-to-end across hardware, data, representations, and benchmarks.
sections.details:
In robot learning, scaling up Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and training world models on massive real-robot demonstration corpora has become the dominant approach. However, two fundamental bottlenecks remain.

The first is the limit of visual reliance. Camera images cannot directly reveal the intensity of fingertip contact forces, whether an object has begun to slip, or whether parts are fully seated. Consequently, operations requiring delicate force modulation—such as folding deformable fabrics or high-precision insertion—frequently fail.

The second is the fragmentation of the tactile modality. Existing tactile sensors span optical camera-based sensors, capacitive arrays, and more, each with distinct output signal formats and spatial resolutions. Data gathered on one sensor cannot be easily transferred to a robot using another, losing the benefits of large-scale pretraining.

N0-Foundation is a comprehensive framework engineered to tackle both problems at their roots. By combining durable sensors and handheld collection interfaces, the 30,000-hour NeoData dataset, the sensor-agnostic 3-axis force field representation model NeoForce, and paired real-world and simulation benchmarks, it aims to establish a true foundation for tactile intelligence.

sections.heading: How does this compare to existing collection tools, representations, and benchmarks?
sections.summary: Prior work spans robot teleoperation, UMI-based collection, large-scale policy learning such as VLAs, and simulation benchmarks. While most previous efforts stay within vision and proprioception, this work stands out by unifying tactile signals into contact force fields alongside a 30,000-hour visuo-tactile demonstration dataset.
sections.details:
This section outlines prior research across four core areas of embodied robotics and clarifies this paper's positioning.

- Hardware and collection methods: Following the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI), which decouples demonstrations from robot arms via handheld grippers, several handheld or wearable tactile collectors have emerged. However, they were restricted to a few specific robot types or relied on raw, sensor-specific outputs.

- Robot manipulation datasets: Datasets like BridgeData V2, Open X-Embodiment, and DROID established scale and diversity, but very few include touch. While relatively large tactile datasets such as AgiBot World and OmniVTA have started to appear, NeoData surpasses them by orders of magnitude—spanning over 30,000 hours (1.4+ million episodes) across 6 embodiments (handheld plus 5 real robot arms) with rigorous quality control.

- Robot learning and tactile representations: Models like RT-1, Diffusion Policy, recent VLAs (such as pi0.5), and world models rely heavily on vision, language, and proprioception. Tactile representation studies, on the other hand, frequently depend on raw images like GelSight. This work is unique in establishing a physical 3-axis ($x, y, z$) contact force field as a universal interchange format that abstracts sensor discrepancies.

- Benchmarks: While simulators like ManiSkill and LIBERO or real-world suites like FurnitureBench and SIMPLER exist, mechanisms to accurately measure and benchmark contact forces have been lacking. This work introduces paired real-world (NeoReal) and simulation (NeoSim) suites to evaluate tactile policies under consistent criteria.

sections.heading: How do durable tactile sensors and the handheld N0-TacUMI enable scalable capture?
sections.summary: The authors developed an optical tactile sensor with a wear-resistant glass panel and mounted it on a handheld collection device called N0-TacUMI. Across 5 real robot arms and the handheld interface (6 embodiments in total), shared coordinate systems and action definitions enable agile, scalable data collection.
sections.details:
To collect tactile data at scale, hardware must endure prolonged friction and contact wear, and operators need ways to collect data rapidly outside fixed workcells.

3.1 Overview: The data acquisition setup spans 6 embodiments: 5 real-world robot arms (Franka Research 3, Piper, ARX X5, UR5e, Flexiv Rizon 4s) and the handheld N0-TacUMI. Real-robot teleoperation ensures faithful robot kinematic profiles, while TacUMI enables abundant, rapid human demonstrations, creating a balanced corpus.

3.2 Tactile sensor: Fingertips employ camera-based optical tactile sensors. A thin wear-resistant glass panel sits on the surface, beneath which an elastomer deforms under external loads, recorded by an internal RGB camera. The sensor reconstructs dense shear and normal pressures across the contact surface from pattern distortions on the elastomer.

3.3 N0-TacUMI: A handheld device designed for agile data collection. It integrates a parallel gripper with two tactile sensors, a 160-degree fisheye camera for a wide workspace view, an infrared tracker for millimeter-precision 6DoF tracking, and a magnetic encoder to measure gripper width. Actions are logged as relative tool center point (TCP) displacements and gripper opening, allowing handheld demonstrations to be directly repurposed as control targets for real robots.

captions.F2: Structure of the handheld collection device N0-TacUMI and fingertip tactile sensors. It integrates a fisheye camera, an infrared tracker, and a magnetic encoder measuring gripper width, while the fingertips house tactile sensors built from wear-resistant glass, an elastomer, and compact RGB cameras.

sections.heading: What makes NeoData a 30,000-hour, 1.4-million-episode visuo-tactile corpus?
sections.summary: The authors built NeoData, spanning 6 embodiments, 450 tasks, and over 30,000 hours, and released OpenNeoData, a 5,000-hour subset. Raw data passes through a stringent quality filtering pipeline, followed by 4-level hierarchical annotations generated using a blend of VLMs and physical signal cues.
sections.details:
4.1 Overview: NeoData was collected by nearly 100 operators and is among the largest real-world robot datasets in existence. It encompasses over 1.4 million episodes, 3.3 billion steps, 8 billion RGB frames, and 10 billion tactile frames. OpenNeoData, covering 5,000 hours and 250+ tasks, is open-sourced to support broader research.

4.2 Data format: Real-robot data logs external fixed camera views, wrist camera views, and tactile images for both fingers ($640\times 360$ resolution), paired with TCP relative translations and target joint angles. Rotations are expressed using continuous 6D representations to avoid discontinuities. TacUMI data similarly records fisheye images, dual tactile frames, relative displacements to future steps, and gripper openings, maintaining a fully unified schema.

4.3 Corpus breakdown: 57% of trajectories were gathered via handheld TacUMI, and the remaining 43% via 5 real robot arms. Objects vary widely, led by cups and boxes. Contact-rich tasks dominate—such as cloth folding, wiping, aligning, inserting, and pouring—where touch is decisive. Episodes average around 80 seconds, capturing long-horizon sequential workflows rather than isolated grasps.

4.4 Curation pipeline: Using raw trajectories directly would introduce noise, so data undergoes a 5-stage check: (1) completeness verification for missing packets, (2) kinematic quality checks removing tracking artifacts, (3) episode-level validation filtering incomplete runs or abnormal lengths, (4) video quality checks removing motion blur or synchronization drift, and (5) transfer feasibility checks ensuring handheld motions can be solved by real robot inverse kinematics (IK).

4.5 Hierarchical annotation: To structure long videos for training, episodes are annotated across 4 tiers: task (L3), subtask (L2), action (L1), and atomic action (L0). A VLM (Gemini-3.5-Flash) generates a task template from reference runs with a single human review pass. Next, temporal boundaries (L0) are pinpointed by combining physical triggers (gripper state changes, tactile pressure spikes) with visual change-point detection. Finally, the VLM assigns semantic labels to each segment, preventing temporal hallucinations typical of VLMs.

captions.F5: The data curation pipeline for NeoData. Raw demonstrations are systematically filtered through five quality criteria: data completeness, trajectory smoothness, episode length and completion, video clarity, and kinematic feasibility (IK solvability) on real robot embodiments.

sections.heading: How does NeoForce turn sensor-dependent images into unified 3-axis force fields?
sections.summary: To overcome hardware-specific imaging variations, the authors defined dense 3-axis contact forces (shear and pressure) as a shared representation. They introduced NeoForce, a foundation model that reconstructs these force fields and models temporal contact dynamics, maintaining consistent physical contact states across diverse tasks.
sections.details:
5.1 Motivation and principles: Tactile sensors vary across hardware in color balance, markers, and mechanical deformation. Relying on raw images forces models to be retrained for every sensor revision. To address this, the authors adhered to three design principles: (1) physical grounding, (2) cross-sensor compatibility, and (3) preservation of spatial contact extent and intensity distributions.

5.2 Definition: Across contact coordinates $(u, v)$, the framework defines a dense 3-axis force field $F_t(u, v) = [f_x(u, v), f_y(u, v), f_z(u, v)]^\top$, combining 2D shear forces ($f_x, f_y$) related to grasp stability and slip with normal pressure ($f_z$). For a parallel gripper, dual fingers yield a 6-channel tensor.

5.3 Implementation: A GoogLeNet-based translation model predicts the 3-axis force field $\hat{F}_t$ from raw images. It is trained on ~4,300 calibrated real-world indentation pairs (using a robot arm and a 6-axis force/torque sensor) combined with finite element analysis (FEA) synthetic simulations.

5.4 NeoForce architecture: Once force fields are obtained, downstream policies need compact, effective features. NeoForce feeds RGB video and tactile force field tokens into a unified Transformer backbone to capture temporal context. Alongside a reconstruction head that recovers force fields, it incorporates latent prediction heads (predicting masked patches and cross-modal visuo-tactile latents).

5.5 Evaluations and findings: Ablations revealed two key insights:
- Finding 1: Adding latent prediction heads reduced absolute force errors (MAE from 0.070 to 0.066, RMSE from 0.095 to 0.089) while preserving spatial contact localization (mIoU 0.966). Visual geometric priors help the model infer masked tactile intensities.
- Finding 2: Across distinct contact regimes—pressing, twisting, grasping, lifting, and holding—NeoForce faithfully recovered ground-truth force fields. Rooting the representation in physical force enables robust generalization across tasks without overfitting.

captions.F7: Architecture of the tactile representation model NeoForce. Tokens from visual frames and tactile force fields are processed by a shared Transformer backbone, concurrently trained via force reconstruction and masked latent prediction to model temporally evolving contact dynamics.
captions.F8: Force field reconstructions across five distinct actions: Press, Twist, Grasp, Lift, and Hold. Top row: camera view; middle row: ground truth force field; bottom row: NeoForce predictions. Contact patch shapes and local force concentrations are captured accurately.

sections.heading: Does tactile feedback decisively improve manipulation on real and simulated benchmarks?
sections.summary: Leading policies were evaluated across the 10 real-world tasks of NeoReal and the 12 simulation tasks of NeoSim. Tactile input significantly improved success rates, with the highest scores achieved when policies received NeoForce force field representations rather than raw tactile images.
sections.details:
6.1 Real-world benchmark (NeoReal): Features 10 contact-critical tasks: box folding, bag packing, cable coiling, whiteboard wiping, paper cup stacking, socket insertion, PCB insertion, bottle uprighting, fruit picking, and bimanual towel folding. In addition to binary success, evaluations track a progressive score (up to 100) measuring partial progress along sub-goals.

6.2 Real-world results: Leading policies, including pi0.5, LingBot-VA, and Fast-WAM, were evaluated after pretraining on NeoData. Even the top performer, pi0.5, averaged a 26.5% success rate (38.1% progressive score), highlighting the difficulty of contact-rich tasks. Tactile integration methods showed striking differences: using pi0.5 as a fixed backbone, the authors evaluated (1) no tactile input, (2) simple raw image concatenation, (3) raw image conditioning on action generation, and (4) NeoForce force field conditioning on action generation. The NeoForce variant achieved a progressive score of 47.5%, outperforming the vision-only baseline (38.1%). Supplying structured physical force fields is clearly superior to presenting raw sensor camera feeds.

6.3 Simulation benchmark (NeoSim): Built on Isaac Sim / Isaac Lab to simulate elastomer deformation and dense contact forces. It includes 4 single-arm tasks (ball pouring, charger plugging/unplugging, USB insertion, fragile chip grasping) and 8 bimanual tasks (screw driving, gear assembly, cup handover, dish stacking, etc.), totaling 12 tasks.

6.4 Simulation results: Over 100 evaluation trials, pi0.5 led with an average success rate of 45.8%. Bimanual tasks proved particularly challenging: while most policies achieved 40–50% on single-arm tasks, bimanual success rates collapsed below 10% (e.g., StarVLA-alpha dropped from 49.3% to 10.1%). Vision alone struggles to maintain mutual grasp stability and coordination during operations like gear assembly or cup handovers. Tactile feedback—which instantly confirms grasp stability and detects excessive forces—emerges as a decisive factor in successful bimanual manipulation.

captions.F9: The 10 tasks in the NeoReal benchmark suite. Tasks like folding cardboard, coiling cables, and inserting PCBs demand precise force modulation and alignment that are difficult to guide purely by sight.

sections.heading: Where does tactile intelligence go from here?
sections.summary: This work introduced tactile collection hardware, the massive NeoData visuo-tactile dataset, the sensor-agnostic NeoForce force field model, and standardized real and simulated benchmarks. Together, they establish a solid foundation for integrating touch into future embodied manipulation.
sections.details:
This research brings tactile sensing to scale within embodied AI, a field largely dominated by vision and language.

Tactile sensors were long treated as cumbersome, specialized hardware in robot learning. However, N0-Foundation demonstrates that handheld collection devices (N0-TacUMI) can make data capture highly efficient. Furthermore, mapping sensor outputs into physical 3-axis force fields enables large-scale learning models to fully harness the benefits of touch.

Challenges remain. The current force representation assumes relatively flat surfaces on two-finger parallel grippers, leaving extensions to multi-fingered dexterous hands and non-optical tactile skins for future work. Narrowing the dynamics gap between NeoSim and real hardware is another active area.

Nonetheless, releasing the 30,000-hour dataset (with its 5,000-hour open-source release), unified representation models, and benchmarks provides a powerful launchpad for overcoming manipulation tasks that vision alone cannot solve.

takeaways: Mapping raw tactile images to physical 3-axis force fields (shear plus pressure) eliminates sensor dependency and boosts downstream policy learning efficiency.
Integrating tactile sensors into handheld devices like TacUMI enables collecting tens of thousands of hours of high-quality, contact-rich demonstrations without being tethered to robot hardware.
While vision-centric policies manage coarse single-arm tasks, their success collapses on contact-rich bimanual coordination, making tactile feedback essential.
Aligning real-world (NeoReal) and simulation (NeoSim) benchmarks under identical force representations allows rigorous, reproducible verification of tactile policies.
limitations: The current force field formulation assumes nearly planar sensor surfaces on parallel grippers; direct application to articulated multi-fingered hands or curved tactile skins remains unverified.
Training the 3-axis force estimator requires both real-world calibration indentations with force/torque sensors and FEA simulations, imposing non-negligible setup costs when onboarding new sensors.

The top-performing policy on the real-world benchmark (NeoReal) achieved an average success rate of only 26.5%, showing that real-time closed-loop contact control still has substantial room for improvement.
